title: Novaya Gazeta Leaves Moscow, Iran Hides Oil in China, Cuba's Shakeup Begins
bluf: Trump says new strikes on Iran are unlikely if Tehran signs a deal. But no mediator has traveled since the midterms, and Iran's Guards say no target is out of range. Russia and Ukraine meet in Abu Dhabi tomorrow, and a Russian outlet reports a ceasefire is not even on the agenda. Novaya Gazeta, Russia's last big independent paper, shut its Moscow servers today and left the city. Cuba's government overhaul took effect today, and ministers have about a month to file their merger plans. Mississippi's mailed ballot deadline is tomorrow, with Colom still ahead by 2,574 votes.

corrections.text: Edition 004 called the military drill that Moscow cited a NATO drill. It is a Coalition of the Willing exercise in Poland, run by the European led force planned for Ukraine, not by NATO.
Edition 004 said Malaysia's former prime minister Najib Razak had gone home under house arrest. A November 7 report says the attorney general is stalling that move, so his status is unclear.

Edition 003 said Japan Tobacco's seized Russian business went to Timur Bolloev, a Putin associate. Japan Tobacco now says a former FSB officer, Sergei Dremov, runs it. He may be the manager rather than the owner.

worldConditions.overall: The Iran war still drives global risk, but both sides are talking about a deal. Tomorrow's Abu Dhabi talks on Ukraine are the week's biggest test. Iraq is caught in the middle, with the US pushing it to close border crossings with Iran.
worldConditions.postureBasis: US and Iranian strikes at a lower level, Russian arms going to Iran, China's drill season near Taiwan, and no ceasefire in Ukraine.

updates.update: Trump said on Nov 8 that new strikes are highly unlikely if Iran signs a strong deal, but Araghchi says mediators have not traveled since the midterms. The blockade is spreading to land, with the US asking Iraq to shut most Iran crossings, while Iraq won a US approved oil lane near Oman. The Guards warned ships not to cooperate with US forces.

iStories reports a ceasefire is not on the Abu Dhabi agenda and the focus is moving to European security. Zakharova said on Nov 7 the coalition drill proves Europe has no place at the table. The drill starts today, and Rosneft has brought back fuel limits in six regions after refinery strikes.

Stephen Miller formally starts as chief of staff today as Congress returns with a December 11 funding deadline and Massie's pending Hegseth impeachment resolution. Mississippi's last day for mailed ballots and affidavit fixes is Tuesday, November 10, with Colom up 2,574 in the latest verified AP count. Alaska's ranked choice tally is set for November 18.

Police put election season scam losses at about NT$20 million in two months, and the Taipei mayor race between Chiang Wan-an and Puma Shen intensified. New chiefs were identified at China's regional war commands after the purge, and Beijing kept pressing Tokyo to retract Prime Minister Takaichi's Taiwan remarks.

Law 186 took effect today, November 9. No list of new ministers or job cuts was found on day one. The next hard date is about December 9, when ministers must give the prime minister their merger timetables.

No new hoax threat or fridge hack attribution found in the window. Germany's response to earlier sabotage is now visible: Russians arriving in Berlin are being questioned by plainclothes officers about the war and mobilization.
No confirmed new development found in the November 7 to 9 window. Unverified leads suggest Lula is prioritizing a constitutional amendment negotiation and will not name ministers this week.

angles.title: The ceasefire, not the bombing, is what keeps Iran fighting
angles.argument: Schwartz says US strikes on about 20,000 targets hurt Iran's military but did not break the regime. He argues the seven month ceasefire handed the initiative back to Tehran. Limited, matched responses taught Iran that Washington will not finish the job.
angles.whyNonObvious: It blames restraint, not escalation, for the war dragging on, which flips the usual post election reading.
angles.counter: Restraint analysts such as Jennifer Kavanagh of Defense Priorities argue more strikes would drain scarce interceptors and leave US forces exposed in Asia for years.

angles.title: Shipping costs will not fall when the war does
angles.outlet: Critical Threats Project, American Enterprise Institute
angles.argument: Moving a 40 foot container cost $4,389 on November 5, against $1,899 in late February. The analysts note that after the 2023 to 2025 Houthi campaign, freight prices stayed high long after attacks stopped. Insurers also raised Red Sea rates and some dropped Saudi linked ships.
angles.whyNonObvious: Markets treat a peace deal as an instant price cut, but insurance and rerouting habits keep costs sticky for months.
angles.counter: Freight trackers saw rates dip last week as Asia to Europe ships drift back to Suez. Carriers also have a big surplus of ships that could push prices down fast once risk eases.

angles.title: The naval blockade made Iraq's border posts a weapon
angles.argument: With sea routes blocked, Iran relies more on trucks crossing into Iraq. Baghdad's closure of one crossing on October 21 therefore bites harder than it would have before the war. Iran's ambassador is lobbying to reopen it.
angles.whyNonObvious: Pressure on Iran now runs partly through small Iraqi customs decisions, not only through US warships.
angles.counter: Iran can reroute through the Kurdistan Region and Turkey, and the ambassador's lobbying, which the same analysts report, suggests Baghdad may bend under pressure from Iran aligned militias.

angles.title: In Abu Dhabi, everyone agrees on the topic and means opposite things
angles.outlet: Institute for the Study of War
angles.argument: US envoy Jared Kushner listed five goals, from crisis hotlines to a long term European security framework with NATO still central. Moscow repeats its 2021 demand that NATO pull back to its 1997 borders and wants Russia and China as guarantors. ISW (the Institute for the Study of War, a hawkish leaning US think tank) says both sides will discuss European security. But their positions cannot fit together.
angles.whyNonObvious: A shared agenda item looks like progress in headlines while hiding the deepest gap in the talks.
angles.counter: Supporters of broad talks, including Norway's prime minister Jonas Gahr Støre, argue only a wide security bargain gives Moscow enough to trade on territory.

angles.title: Russia's elite is now paying for the war too
angles.outlet: Institute for the Study of War
angles.argument: Russia's two houses of parliament plan staff cuts of 10 to 20%, after a 15% civil service cut in March. The stated reason is growing deficits and nonessential social spending. ISW reads it as part of a wider push to move state money to the war.
angles.whyNonObvious: Cuts aimed at the political class rather than the public are a quiet sign that budget pressure has reached the top.
angles.counter: Russian officials frame it as routine efficiency, and the sums are small next to defense spending, so it may be more symbol than strain.

angles.title: COP31 may be a trade fight dressed as a climate summit
angles.argument: China wants talks on trade rules that block clean technology, aiming at Western tariffs on its panels, batteries and cars. African countries want trade on the formal agenda too. European countries, defending their carbon border tax, are expected to resist.
angles.whyNonObvious: The real split in Antalya may be over who sells the green economy, not how fast emissions fall.
angles.counter: EU negotiators argue trade measures belong at the World Trade Organization, and that climate talks should not become a back door to unwind border carbon pricing.

angles.title: The adaptation fight is over a number that still leaves most of the gap
angles.argument: Rich countries blocked a target to triple adaptation money by 2035. Even tripled, it would reach $85 to 120 billion a year against needs of about $305 billion. The indicators meant to track progress were cut from 100 to 59.
angles.whyNonObvious: Winning the headline target would still leave poor countries short by about two thirds, and fewer indicators make the shortfall harder to prove.
angles.counter: Developed countries argue development banks and private money will fill the gap, and that a fixed public target creates obligations their parliaments will not pass.

angles.title: Moscow treats Iran and Ukraine as one bargaining table
angles.argument: The author argues Russia links the Iran and Ukraine files into one negotiating space. Sanctions relief for Moscow in a Ukraine deal could then indirectly help Tehran's main backer. He also warns a war over nuclear weapons could weaken the taboo on biological weapons, which are cheaper and harder to trace.
angles.whyNonObvious: It suggests a Ukraine deal in Abu Dhabi could carry hidden costs for the Iran war, and the reverse.
angles.counter: Others note Russia's help to Iran has been limited and transactional, and that Moscow gains mainly from high oil prices, not from an Iranian win. The outlet is small and its sourcing is thin.

stateNarratives.outlet: Russian Foreign Ministry (Maria Zakharova), via Expert.ru
stateNarratives.claim: The coalition drill held right before Abu Dhabi proves Europeans have no business at the negotiating table. Any foreign troops in Ukraine would be a military intervention and legitimate targets.
stateNarratives.counterpoint: The UK Ministry of Defence says the force would deploy only after fighting ends and at Ukraine's request, with no peacekeeping role. Peskov himself has said Russia will eventually need to talk European security with Europeans.

stateNarratives.claim: Security guarantees in Abu Dhabi can only be mutual. Indivisible security, meaning no state's safety at another's expense, is the cornerstone of Russia's position.
stateNarratives.counterpoint: Moscow used the same 'indivisible security' language in 2021 to demand NATO pull back from Eastern Europe. Kyiv wants guarantees modeled on NATO's Article 5 and backed by the US Congress.

stateNarratives.claim: Europe cannot join the Abu Dhabi format and is taking too long to choose who would negotiate for it.
stateNarratives.counterpoint: US officials met France, Germany, the UK, the EU and NATO in Brussels before Abu Dhabi, so Europe has input through Washington. Nordic and Baltic leaders are openly split on talking to Putin, which gives Moscow's point some basis.

stateNarratives.claim: Novaya Gazeta leaving its office of 30 years is an ordinary 'rotation', not a closure forced by the state.
stateNarratives.counterpoint: CPJ documents the cut off of its donations, eviction from its office, the foreign agent label, a search of the editor's home and a reporter under house arrest, all in 2026.

stateNarratives.outlet: PRC Ministry of Foreign Affairs (spokesperson Guo Jiakun)
stateNarratives.claim: Beijing blames Tokyo for the poor state of relations. It says Japan's first job is to correct its wrong words and deeds on Taiwan, meaning Prime Minister Takaichi's remarks, and to face its history.
stateNarratives.relatedTo: Japan and China dispute over Takaichi's Taiwan remarks
stateNarratives.counterpoint: Tokyo says Takaichi described when Japan's own self defense law could apply and that its Taiwan policy has not changed. Japanese business and political delegations keep visiting China, so ties are strained but not frozen.

stateNarratives.outlet: PRC Ministry of Foreign Affairs (spokesperson Guo Jiakun)
stateNarratives.claim: Beijing says its cooperation with Cuba is completely legitimate. It opposes US unilateral sanctions and long arm jurisdiction and promises to take all necessary measures to protect Chinese companies.
stateNarratives.relatedTo: New US sanctions on Chinese firms accused of military supplies to Cuba
stateNarratives.counterpoint: Washington says the firms supplied military items to Cuba. Beijing did not address what the firms actually sold.

stateNarratives.outlet: IRNA (state news agency), via Iran International
stateNarratives.claim: Ali Balali, an adviser to the Guards' missile force, said Iranian missiles now hit precisely at about 2,000 km. At the program's start the range was about 300 km.
stateNarratives.relatedTo: Missile range and threats beyond the region
stateNarratives.counterpoint: The same day the Guards said they had dropped their 2,000 km cap, yet Iran is not known to own missiles that fly further. US officials say space launch technology could be adapted, but no longer range system has been shown.

stateNarratives.outlet: Kayhan (hardline daily whose editor is named by the Supreme Leader), via Iran International
stateNarratives.claim: Kayhan highlighted an estimated 127 billion euros in European losses from the Hormuz closure as proof that Tehran is winning.
stateNarratives.counterpoint: Iran's own labor news agency says basic household costs nearly doubled in seven months, and Brent fell 17% last week as markets priced a deal. Earlier tracking found Hormuz traffic slowed but did not collapse.

stateNarratives.claim: The government calls its restructuring a response to the economic crisis and US pressure. It says the goal is a leaner, more efficient state.
stateNarratives.relatedTo: Law 186 government overhaul, in force November 9
stateNarratives.counterpoint: The law text sets no job cuts, names no ministers and changes no US sanctions. Independent outlets note it is silent on what happens to staff of merged units, after the prime minister announced 92,000 post cuts in July.
stateNarratives.date: 2026 (not opened, exact date not confirmed, likely around the July approval)

underRadar.headline: Iranian oil may be hiding in Chinese tanks, not just at sea
underRadar.summary: A leaked document seen by Iran International says Iran uses terminals and storage inside China to keep sanctioned tankers moving. No companies or ports are named publicly yet.
underRadar.whyUndercovered: Blockade coverage tracks ships at sea. Onshore storage in China is harder to see and politically awkward for Washington during trade talks.
underRadar.coverage: Single source, Persian language opposition channel.

underRadar.headline: Germany is quietly interviewing arriving Russians about the war
underRadar.summary: Plainclothes officers at Berlin airport are inviting Russian arrivals to 'voluntary' interviews about mobilization, inflation and the war. At least one woman learned only midway that she could refuse. The airport says this is not its staff's job, and German police did not reply.
underRadar.whyUndercovered: Reported only by a small Russian language exile outlet, and Germany has not announced the practice.
underRadar.coverage: Holod, republished by Meduza. No German outlet found.

underRadar.headline: Two million Myanmar migrants sign on to refuse the junta's ID
underRadar.summary: Myanmar workers in Thailand are boycotting the junta's identity certificate, which forces them to send home a quarter of their pay. Only about 15,000 applied against an expected thousands per day.
underRadar.whyUndercovered: Migrant labor stories in Thailand rarely reach English language media, and the boycott is organized through worker networks, not the armed resistance.

underRadar.headline: The Caspian is too shallow for the West's favorite Russia bypass
underRadar.summary: A Kazakh environmentalist warns the falling Caspian Sea level threatens the Trans-Caspian trade route that skips Russia.
underRadar.whyUndercovered: Corridor coverage focuses on deals and summits, not water levels.

underRadar.headline: Sudan's breadbasket is losing crops to a petrol shortage
underRadar.summary: Farmers in the Gezira scheme, Sudan's largest irrigated farm area, say maize is dying because pumps have no fuel. Food prices in Gezira towns have jumped, with a sack of sesame near 860,000 Sudanese pounds.
underRadar.whyUndercovered: Coverage of Sudan focuses on Darfur and Kordofan fighting. Gezira is under army control and looks calm from outside.
underRadar.coverage: Only Radio Dabanga found. No wire coverage seen.

underRadar.headline: Researchers say a Russian operation altered local TV news to smear Democratic Senate candidates
underRadar.summary: Researchers tied altered local news clips about James Talarico in Texas, Sherrod Brown in Ohio and Troy Jackson in Maine to Storm-1516. That is a Russian influence campaign active since 2023. Real Cleveland and Bangor TV reports were edited to add abuse claims.
underRadar.whyUndercovered: It surfaced the week before the vote and was buried by results coverage. Fact checks ran on candidate specific pages, not as one story.
underRadar.coverage: PolitiFact (Oct 30) and a FinChannel summary (Nov 2). No national TV follow up found.

conspiracies.claim: Under Israeli pressure, Trump will use a nuclear weapon on Iran's buried enrichment site during the lame duck period.
conspiracies.whereSpreading: Tucker Carlson's show, X, Daily Beast coverage, antiwar Substacks on left and right.
conspiracies.origin: Tucker Carlson on Sunday Nov 1. He said it could happen as early as the weekend after the midterms.
conspiracies.whyBelieved: Carlson is seen as close to Trump's circle. Trump said anything is possible on further strikes. Moon of Alabama separately predicted a strike around the Nov 8 to 9 new moon.
conspiracies.caseFor: Trump has not ruled out more strikes. AP reported US officials told Middle East allies to prepare for renewed strikes. Iraq's nuclear regulator has publicly modeled fallout from a strike on Iran's Pickaxe Mountain site.
conspiracies.caseAgainst: Carlson gave no source. The Daily Beast called the claim unverified. Israeli press reported on Nov 8 that no major US buildup was detected. The first named weekend passed with only minor US strikes reported.
conspiracies.unknowns: Whether Carlson had a real source. Whether Israel's change of government under Gadi Eisenkot changes the pressure.

conspiracies.claim: Federal health officials knew their safety system could not detect mRNA vaccine harms and hid it, while medical examiners privately doubted safety.
conspiracies.whereSpreading: The Defender, NaturalNews, health freedom Substacks and Telegram channels.
conspiracies.origin: What is new: the medical examiner emails are now paired with a BMJ (a British medical journal) investigation by David Willman and FDA (the US Food and Drug Administration) emails said to come from Senate subpoenas.
conspiracies.whyBelieved: It rests on real documents and a respected journal. It fits long held distrust of the FDA and the CDC.
conspiracies.caseFor: The BMJ reports a masking flaw in the FDA's tool. An internal FDA email from October 2023 acknowledged the limit. Medical examiners did discuss deaths after vaccination.
conspiracies.caseAgainst: The emails show doubt as well as concern. One chief examiner wrote she doubted a link. A design flaw in a screening tool does not by itself show hidden harm. The CDC publicly acknowledged a myocarditis risk in 2021.
conspiracies.unknowns: What the full Senate document set shows. Whether the fixed algorithm would have flagged anything new.
conspiracies.watch: Senate health committee hearings, any FDA statement on the BMJ piece, new state records releases.
conspiracies.relatedTo: The Defender medical examiner emails (published earlier).
conspiracies.audience: Vaccine skeptics, parents of injured people, Make America Healthy Again supporters.
conspiracies.forumChatter: No researcher or press description of forum spread found in this run.

conspiracies.claim: Democratic Senate candidates James Talarico, Sherrod Brown and Troy Jackson abused students or staff, as shown in local TV reports.
conspiracies.whereSpreading: X, through what researchers call a rotating cast of paid influencers.
conspiracies.origin: Researchers attribute the videos to Storm-1516, a Russian influence campaign also active in 2024.
conspiracies.whyBelieved: The clips look like real local news. Jackson's real documented outbursts gave one clip a factual hook.
conspiracies.caseFor: Jackson's temper as Maine Senate President was reported by WABI-TV. The clips use real stations' branding and reporters.
conspiracies.caseAgainst: The original Cleveland 19 report did not contain the abuse claim. Named former Brown staffers denied it. PolitiFact found the Talarico video was AI generated and impersonated a real man. Clemson's Darren Linvill and the firm Graphika tied the accounts to Storm-1516.
conspiracies.unknowns: Who pays the influencers. Whether the operation resumes during certification or the January swearing in.
conspiracies.watch: New clips aimed at winners, especially in close races still being counted.
conspiracies.audience: Voters already distrustful of Democratic candidates and of results.
conspiracies.forumChatter: Per the article, fewer than 7,000 people mentioned Troy Jackson on X on Oct 28, and about a quarter were discussing the Russian narrative.

conspiracies.claim: The November 17 national emergency alert test is the starting signal for the planned crisis governments are preparing people for.
conspiracies.whereSpreading: Not yet observed. Expected on prepper sites, ZeroHedge comments and Telegram.
conspiracies.origin: Anticipated. FEMA (the US disaster agency)'s nationwide test of TV, radio and phone alerts is set for Nov 17 at about 2:20 pm Eastern, the first in three years.
conspiracies.whyBelieved: It lands on top of the stockpile story, Bongino's 30 day advice and the Doomsday Plane flight. The last national test in 2023 drew similar online claims.
conspiracies.caseFor: The test is real and dated. Governments really are issuing preparedness advice.
conspiracies.caseAgainst: The test is required under federal rules and was announced in September. The message says no action is needed. Official advice in the US and UK is a few days of supplies, not a month.
conspiracies.unknowns: Whether a major outlet or influencer ties the test to the crisis story before Nov 17.
conspiracies.watch: Mentions of the test by Bongino, Corbett, OffGuardian or ZeroHedge this week. The backup date is December 3.
conspiracies.relatedTo: Corbett synchronized warnings, ZeroHedge Doomsday Plane, Bongino 30 day warning.
conspiracies.audience: Preppers, Covid era skeptics, Iran war watchers.
conspiracies.forumChatter: None yet. On Oct 30, Texas A&M risk expert Angela Clendenin told Sinclair stations that Bongino's warning sent people down a rabbit hole.

items.headline: Miller starts as chief of staff with Congress lost
items.summary: Stephen Miller, the architect of Trump's immigration crackdown, takes over from Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff today, November 9. The job lets him control who briefs Trump and coordinate Homeland Security, Justice and budget officials. Republicans split in public: Rep. Marlin Stutzman called it a horrible decision, while Sen. Mike Lee praised Miller's law enforcement record.
items.assessment: Choosing an agency operator over a dealmaker signals the next two years will run through executive action and enforcement money Congress already approved. Democratic subpoenas will likely aim at Miller himself, since every agency decision now passes through him.

items.headline: Hegseth impeachment vote can be forced as the House returns
items.summary: Rep. Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican who lost his primary, filed eight impeachment articles against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in September. They cite the Iran war without approval from Congress, deadly strikes on suspected drug boats and the capture of Nicolás Maduro. Speaker Mike Johnson sent the House home before a vote and promised to table it on return. Gray TV reported that several Republican sources now expect impeachment to pass, while Trump wants Hegseth to fight.
items.assessment: The first floor test is a motion to table, so any Republican voting no breaks with Trump on the record. We put the chance the House impeaches before January at about 40%, but removal needs 67 senators, so conviction is under 5%.

items.headline: Lame duck opens with a December 11 shutdown deadline
items.summary: Congress returns today for its last weeks under Republican control. Federal funding runs out December 11, and the yearly defense policy bill still has to pass. Massie also told The Hill he expects to force a follow up vote on the Epstein files this week through a discharge petition, a tool that bypasses leadership.
items.assessment: With both chambers flipping in January, Democrats have little reason to give ground now. A short stopgap into early 2027 is more likely than a full year deal, which hands the new majorities the first big spending fight.

items.headline: Mississippi Senate count hits Tuesday cutoff with Colom up 2,574
items.summary: Democrat Scott Colom led Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by 2,574 votes in Associated Press figures on Friday evening. We found no newer verified count. Tuesday, November 10, is the last day for mailed ballots to arrive. It is also the last day to fix rejected affidavit ballots, the provisional ballots cast when a voter's eligibility is in question. Counties must certify by November 13.
items.assessment: Counted affidavit ballots broke heavily for Colom, about 80% in Oktibbeha County, so Hyde-Smith's path depends on which affidavit ballots are accepted. Her campaign says it only wants them kept separate for review, but Mississippi has no recount process, so any challenge goes straight to court.

items.headline: Alaska waits for the November 18 ranked count
items.summary: Democrat Mary Peltola and Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan are under one point apart, and neither has a majority. Alaska will run its ranked choice tally on November 18, after all eligible ballots are counted. Trump said votes for a second candidate named Dan Sullivan should go to the senator, Axios reported.
items.assessment: Under ranked choice, the lesser Sullivan will likely be dropped early and his voters' next choices then count anyway. Trump's demand only matters for ballots that listed no second choice, so it works better as a grievance than as a source of votes.

alsoNoted.headline: Mississippi GOP chair says the party will accept a Colom win if he wins
alsoNoted.source: The Hill, via Just Security Early Edition
alsoNoted.note: Softer than chair Mike Hurst's earlier pledge to fight hard over the count.

alsoNoted.headline: Rubio reportedly weighing an exit from State, which calls it a hoax
alsoNoted.source: Bloomberg and The Hill, via Just Security Early Edition

alsoNoted.headline: Schumer says Democrats will block a hard right Supreme Court pick
alsoNoted.source: AP, via Just Security Early Edition
alsoNoted.note: Matters only if a seat opens before January or in the new Senate.

alsoNoted.headline: Mississippi Senate ballot fight live tracker: counties certify by November 13

items.headline: Trump says new Iran strikes are highly unlikely if Tehran signs
items.summary: Trump told CNN by phone that more strikes on Iran depend on Tehran signing a very strong agreement. He said it is highly unlikely new attacks will be needed. Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said the mediators from Qatar and Pakistan have not traveled since the US midterms and asked for patience.
items.assessment: Oil traders are already pricing a deal that nobody is negotiating in person yet. Brent fell 17% last week, which weakens the oil pressure Iran was counting on to win concessions.
items.source: Asharq Al-Awsat (Reuters reports on oil and the G7 meeting)

items.headline: US asks Iraq to close all but two border crossings with Iran
items.summary: Iraq's foreign minister Fuad Hussein told Al Jazeera that the US Treasury asked Baghdad to shut every Iran crossing except two. One of the two is in the Kurdistan Region. Hussein said closing them would hurt Iraq's economy and talks with Washington continue.
items.assessment: The US sea blockade of Iran is now being pushed onto land, and Iraq is where it leaks most. Leaving a Kurdish crossing open keeps Erbil on side while squeezing trade that runs through Shia militia held areas in the south.

items.headline: Iraq gets a US approved shipping lane near Oman for its oil
items.summary: Iraq reached an understanding with the US on Sunday to send its oil exports through Hormuz using a lane near Oman. Foreign minister Fuad Hussein put Iraq's losses from the war and blocked exports at $60 billion. Separately, Iran's own shipping authority for the strait lists tankers it calls non compliant, and about 30% of the cargo on that list is Iraqi, according to TankerTrackers.
items.assessment: Iraqi tankers now need a green light from both Washington and Tehran to move. That makes Baghdad the first country formally caught between two rival permit systems in the same waterway.

items.headline: Leaked paper says Iran is using Chinese oil terminals to dodge sanctions
items.summary: Iran International, a London based Persian language channel opposed to the Islamic Republic, says it obtained a confidential document. It reports that Iran is using oil terminals and storage tanks inside China to keep its sanctioned tankers working. The outlet cites Oil Ministry sources but the public text names no companies or ports.
items.assessment: If accurate, Iranian oil is being parked inside China rather than at sea, which blunts the US naval blockade. Any US move against those terminals would turn the Iran war into a direct trade fight with Beijing.

items.headline: Revolutionary Guards warn ships not to work with US forces
items.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guards, the elite military force that runs Iran's side of the strait, said three tankers were on fire in Hormuz. They then warned ships against cooperating with US forces. The same day, Iran's Guards spokesman said any place seen as a serious threat could become a target.
items.assessment: The warning is aimed at the new US managed lanes, including Iraq's. Ship captains who follow US instructions now face a stated Iranian penalty, which may push insurers to price both sides' rules.

items.headline: Hardliners in burial shrouds accuse the Guards of defying Iran's leader
items.summary: A group of hardline women wearing white burial shrouds rallied outside Revolutionary Guards headquarters in Tehran. They accused the armed forces of ignoring Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei and demanded revenge for threats against him. The video came from Tabnak, a news site linked to Mohsen Rezaei, Iran's security council secretary.
items.assessment: Pressure from the regime's own base is running against restraint, not for it. A deal with Washington would have to survive people who already accuse the military of going soft.

items.headline: New: Iran executes three Karaj protesters as more death sentences follow
items.summary: Iran's judiciary said on Nov 8 it had executed Hassan Divband, Hamid Kazemi and Reza Zanganeh, arrested during January protests in Karaj, a city west of Tehran. The rights group HRANA reported new death sentences in Mashhad and the Shandiz case, which now has six. Iran International also reported, from one unnamed source, that a 17 year old killed in January had been tortured at age 13.
items.assessment: Executions are rising while Tehran talks peace abroad. The state appears to be using the war to close out the January protest cases before any deal brings outside scrutiny.
items.source: Iran International (citing Iran's judiciary and HRANA)

alsoNoted.headline: Iran's envoy in Moscow details a gas swap through Azerbaijan and a large pipeline plan
alsoNoted.note: New detail beyond the Rezaei and Putin meeting. Ambassador Kazem Jalali said Russia would supply northern Azerbaijan while Azerbaijan sends gas to Iran. He described a pipeline of 110 billion cubic meters a year, built in two to three years.

alsoNoted.headline: Guards adviser says Iranian missiles hit precisely at about 2,000 km (IRNA claim)
alsoNoted.note: Said the same day the Guards announced they dropped their self set range cap. The two lines pull in different directions.

alsoNoted.headline: Cost of basic household needs nearly doubled in seven months, labor news agency says
alsoNoted.note: ILNA put monthly needs at 85 million tomans. Pensioners and contract workers are protesting.

alsoNoted.headline: Iran's industry minister asks to delay car safety rules as road deaths top 10,000 in six months

items.headline: As the Knesset sits, ultra Orthodox parties hold the swing seats
items.summary: Israel's new parliament is due to be sworn in on Nov 10. Gadi Eisenkot, a former army chief now leading the opposition, has the first try at a government but lacks 61 seats without Arab parties. The two ultra Orthodox parties, Shas and United Torah Judaism, hold 13 seats and broke with Netanyahu over a failed draft exemption law. Avigdor Liberman, long their fiercest critic, now says he will talk to them.
items.assessment: Eisenkot's easiest path to power runs through the religious parties, not the Arab ones. The likely price is a softer military draft deal, the very issue the opposition campaigned on.

items.headline: Winter rain floods Gaza tent camps in Deir al-Balah
items.summary: Heavy rain flooded tents of displaced families in Deir al-Balah in central Gaza, soaking mattresses and turning paths to mud. More than 1.6 million Palestinians still live in tents or makeshift shelters. Almost the whole population has lost its home in the war that followed the October 7, 2023 attack.
items.assessment: Gaza's second winter under tents is starting while Israel has no government able to approve reconstruction steps. Coalition talks in Jerusalem could leave shelter decisions frozen for weeks.

alsoNoted.headline: Reports say Netanyahu pushed Trump to restart the Iran war right after the midterms
alsoNoted.source: Iran International (citing Israel's Channel 12 and CNN)
alsoNoted.note: New beyond the earlier report of a planned pre election operation. Trump reportedly wanted more time for talks. The prime minister's office denied the Channel 12 report.

alsoNoted.headline: Israel's election committee certified the results and found no fraud

items.headline: New: Iraq's prime minister cancels Mosul airport contracts and vows armed groups will go
items.summary: Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi canceled contracts held by three companies at Mosul Airport over links to armed groups. He handed the work to foreign firms. In a Sadr City visit he said he would not let armed groups remain. Kataib Hezbollah, an Iran aligned militia, answered by mocking his brother Hassan, who runs media and security in his office.
items.assessment: Disarmament is being bought, not forced. Factions that gave up weapons reportedly got posts in ministries and embassies, while holdouts face lost contracts and a reported US warning of strikes.

items.headline: New: Khor Mor drone likely came from near Tuz Khurmatu, source says
items.summary: A local source told Shafaq News the drone that hit Kurdistan's Khor Mor gas field probably took off from hills near Tuz Khurmatu in Saladin province. The field is run by Pearl Petroleum, a group that includes UAE based Dana Gas. Gas output and exports stopped fully and no one has claimed the attack.
items.assessment: Tuz Khurmatu sits outside the Kurdistan Region in federally held ground where state backed militia units operate. If confirmed, Baghdad cannot blame the launch on territory it does not control.

items.headline: Yemen's ground war heats up in Lahj as Houthis claim 27 killed near Sanaa
items.summary: Yemen's Saudi backed government army says it retook positions on the Al-Mudharabah front in Lahj province and fought in Taiz, Al-Jawf and Marib. It claims 875 operations on Saturday. The Houthi run health ministry said airstrikes on a village near Sanaa killed at least 27, mostly women and children, and blamed Saudi Arabia. Saudi Arabia did not respond to AP.
items.assessment: The Saudi and Houthi fight is now a ground war again, not just missiles. That ties down Riyadh at the moment it wants to look like a peacemaker at the G7.

items.headline: Saudi foreign minister joins G7 talks in Paris on Iran and Ukraine
items.summary: G7 foreign ministers opened a two day meeting in Paris on Nov 9, moved at the last minute from Marseille. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is attending both days. Saudi Arabia's foreign minister arrived to join. Iran's demands still include sanctions relief, frozen funds and war reparations, while Washington wants nuclear issues in the first round.
items.assessment: Riyadh is sitting with the West on Iran while Houthi missiles still hit Saudi cities. Its presence suggests the Gulf wants a say in any Hormuz deal rather than being handed one.

items.headline: Two trains collide in Giza, killing seven and injuring over 100
items.summary: A train bound for Fayoum crashed into the back of a train heading to Aswan in the al-Ayyat district of Giza, south of Cairo. Seven people died and more than 100 were hurt, according to Egypt's Transportation Ministry. Saudi Arabia sent condolences.
items.assessment: Rail crashes have long been a pressure point for Egypt's government. With Mada Masr ordered closed, the independent outlet that most often dug into such failures is not there to investigate this one.

alsoNoted.headline: Houthis claim six missile and drone operations on oil and military sites in Saudi Arabia and Yemen
alsoNoted.note: Claim by Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree. Not verified.

alsoNoted.headline: Khor Mor production suspended after a drone hit an LPG storage tank
alsoNoted.note: Same strike already covered. Only new detail is the storage tank hit.

items.headline: Novaya Gazeta switches off its servers and leaves Moscow today
items.summary: Novaya Gazeta, the Nobel winning independent paper, is shutting its Moscow newsroom on November 9 after 30 years in the same office. The state cut off its donation platform, evicted it, and labeled it a foreign agent in September. The team is moving an archive of about 94,000 articles to GitHub, the code sharing site.
items.assessment: This ends the last well known independent newsroom still legally inside Russia. Exile outlets like Novaya Gazeta Europe now carry the whole job, which makes on the ground reporting harder to verify.
items.source: Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) and iStories

items.headline: Abu Dhabi round will not discuss a ceasefire, iStories reports
items.summary: The exiled investigative outlet iStories reports that a ceasefire is off the agenda for the November 10 to 11 talks. It says the focus is shifting from Ukraine itself to European security more broadly. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on November 3 that any security guarantees can only be mutual.
items.assessment: Russia added Sergei Ryabkov, its arms control and US relations diplomat, to the team. That fits a push to trade on Europe's wider security setup rather than the front line. A prisoner exchange remains the likeliest concrete result, with about a 5% chance of any ceasefire announcement from this round.

items.headline: Russian military channels post AI made front videos of towns Ukraine holds
items.summary: iStories reports that Russian armed forces are publishing front line videos made with artificial intelligence. The clips are used to announce the capture of towns that Ukraine still controls. The outlet's article was not opened, so the specific channels and towns are not confirmed here.
items.assessment: Fake capture claims on the eve of talks help Moscow argue the map is already moving its way. For open source analysts, every Russian capture video this week needs a location and date check before use.

items.headline: Rosneft brings back fuel purchase limits in six regions
items.summary: Rosneft, Russia's largest state oil company, has reintroduced limits on how much fuel drivers can buy at its gas stations. iStories says the limits now apply in six regions. They follow new Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refineries.
items.assessment: Rationing at the pump is something ordinary Russians feel directly, unlike battlefield claims. It gives Kyiv a pressure point to show in Abu Dhabi, and gives Moscow a reason to seek an energy strike pause.

items.headline: Moscow police detain several hundred people in a Kitai-gorod raid
items.summary: iStories reports the largest police raid yet in Kitai-gorod, a busy district in central Moscow. Several hundred people were detained on November 8. Who was targeted and why is not confirmed here, because the article was not opened.
items.assessment: Mass sweeps in Moscow are often used to find men for military service or to check migrants. Either way, the scale suggests security services now feel free to run large raids in the capital itself.

items.headline: JTI (Japan Tobacco International) says its seized Russian business went to a former FSB (Russia's security service) officer
items.summary: Japan Tobacco International (JTI) confirmed that management of its seized Russian assets went to Sergei Dremov. iStories describes him as a former officer of the FSB, Russia's main security service. An earlier report had named Putin associate Timur Bolloev as the recipient.
items.assessment: The two names may reflect a manager and an owner, or a change of plan. Either way, a security service veteran running a large foreign business shows how seized Western assets are being handed to trusted insiders.

items.headline: Georgia's prime minister calls China 'the only peaceful superpower'
items.summary: Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze praised China while hosting Chinese Vice President Han Zheng in Tbilisi. The same day, a Russian farm inspection team visited fruit facilities in Gori while Russia keeps a ban on Georgian drinks.
items.assessment: Georgia's ruling Georgian Dream party is filling the gap left by cooling EU ties with Beijing, while Moscow uses trade bans to keep leverage. Tbilisi is hedging toward both, not just toward Russia.

items.headline: Erdoğan visits Azerbaijan for Victory Day after weeks of strain
items.summary: Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan visited Azerbaijan on its Victory Day, which marks the 2020 war win over Armenia. He and President Ilham Aliyev praised their alliance. OC Media says ties had been strained for weeks before the trip.
items.assessment: The public warmth is a repair job. Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu is also reportedly due in Baku, so Aliyev is balancing Ankara and Israel at a time when Turkey and Israel are openly hostile.

alsoNoted.headline: Ukrainian military intelligence says 55 died in a Russian strike on Kamyshevakha and it has identified the Russian personnel involved
alsoNoted.note: Not opened. Date of the strike itself not confirmed. Large toll worth checking against Ukrainian sources.

alsoNoted.headline: Russian woman wounded in the Kraków shooting is stable. New since Nov 8, the gunman died in hospital on Nov 9
alsoNoted.note: Kraków shooting already published Nov 8. Only the gunman's death is new.

alsoNoted.headline: Azerbaijan plans house to house counts of personal tech devices from 2027
alsoNoted.note: Undated on the homepage. Include only if dated elsewhere.

alsoNoted.headline: Armenia's opposition campaigns against proposed constitutional changes
alsoNoted.note: Undated on the homepage. Follows the opposition unification already published Nov 7.

items.headline: Coalition drill opens in Poland with jets rehearsing guarding Ukrainian skies
items.summary: About 2,800 troops from 11 countries start Exercise Koalicja near Nowa Dęba, southeastern Poland, today through November 22. Britain and France lead it, under British Lt. Gen. Tom Bateman. RAF Typhoon jets will practice protecting civilian flights if Ukraine reopens its airspace, and Turkish officers will plan clearing sea mines from Istanbul.
items.assessment: This is a Coalition of the Willing exercise, not a formal NATO one. It rehearses a force that only deploys after fighting stops, which is exactly the clause Moscow says it will treat as an invasion.

items.headline: Russians landing in Berlin face 'voluntary' interviews about war and mobilization
items.summary: Russian citizens arriving at Berlin airport are being taken aside by plainclothes officers after passport control. Two women told Holod, an independent Russian outlet, they were asked about mobilization, inflation and their views on the war. One interview lasted about an hour.
items.assessment: Germany promised tighter checks on Russians after the Leipzig airport cargo plane sabotage it blamed on Moscow. Turning arrivals into informal intelligence interviews is the quiet, unannounced form of that promise.

items.headline: Slovakia restarts a joint commission with Russia after five years
items.summary: A Russian and Slovak government commission met again on October 26 after a five year pause, with oil, gas and nuclear fuel on the agenda. A Novaya Gazeta commentary calls Prime Minister Robert Fico a self appointed go between for Moscow, Kyiv and Brussels. At home, the opposition seeks a no confidence vote on Foreign Minister Juraj Blanár.
items.assessment: With Orbán gone from power in Hungary since April, Fico is now the EU's most Moscow friendly leader. A Polish think tank warns his talks with Moscow could leak internal EU sanctions debates, though no evidence of that has surfaced.

items.headline: Slovak prosecutors reopen the probe into MiG-29 jets sent to Ukraine
items.summary: Slovakia's prosecutor has reopened an investigation into the 2023 transfer of MiG-29 fighter jets to Ukraine, made by the previous government. Slovakia ended state military aid to Kyiv but still allows commercial arms sales. On November 2 it also joined an international group working to return deported Ukrainian children.
items.assessment: The probe lets Fico's camp paint its predecessors as reckless while still profiting from arms exports. Mixed signals like the children's coalition keep Bratislava inside the EU mainstream on paper.

alsoNoted.headline: France puts an Ingush man on trial for the 2023 killing of a teacher, and relatives once suspected are cleared
alsoNoted.note: Not opened. Likely the Arras school attack case.

alsoNoted.headline: France sends about 1,100 troops to the Poland drill per Kyiv Post, but 1,500 per TASS citing reports
alsoNoted.note: Small figure gap between outlets. The UK Ministry of Defence says the force would not do peacekeeping or ceasefire monitoring.

items.headline: Serbia's Alta Banka goes bankrupt, raising spillover fears
items.summary: The French Treasury's regional office reports that Alta Banka, a Serbian bank, has gone bankrupt. It warns of contagion to Serbia's real economy. North Macedonia's central bank is also watching the crisis closely.
items.assessment: A bank failure in Serbia during a political transition tests whether the new parliamentary majority can manage a financial shock. Cross border exposure into North Macedonia makes it a regional story, not just a Serbian one.
items.source: French Treasury (DG Trésor) Western Balkans brief

items.headline: Bosnia still has no EU chief negotiator two years after candidacy
items.summary: Bosnia and Herzegovina has not named a chief negotiator for EU membership talks two years after becoming a candidate. The European Commission's November 4 report reads this as disengagement and records setbacks on basic reforms. Serbia also slid back, while Kosovo and North Macedonia stalled.
items.assessment: A missing negotiator is a choice, not an oversight. It lets Republika Srpska's leaders block the EU track without a public veto, and Hungary's new government has already cut their subsidies.
items.source: French Treasury (DG Trésor) Western Balkans brief

items.headline: Albania could get early access to some EU policies before joining
items.summary: The Commission published a membership roadmap for Albania and set June 2027 as the target to sign Montenegro's accession treaty. Under a proposed gradual integration plan, Albania may gain access to some EU programs before full membership, with conditions.
items.assessment: Early access lets Brussels reward the two front runners without waiting on unanimous treaty votes. It also widens the gap with Serbia and Bosnia, which raises pressure on Belgrade's new majority.
items.source: French Treasury (DG Trésor) Western Balkans brief

alsoNoted.headline: US extends Serbia's NIS oil company license again. Gigatron electronics chain sold to Slovenia's Bidigital Investments
Kosovo drafts a €4.7 billion spending plan for 2027. North Macedonia plans a 3.5% deficit
Montenegro flags credit and real estate risks as its deficit comes in below forecast

items.headline: Scammers cash in on Taiwan's campaign season, police say
items.summary: Taiwan's Criminal Investigation Bureau, the national police detective agency, says election themed scams cost victims about NT$20.15 million (about US$615,000) in two months. October alone brought 87 cases. Fake offers of free campaign umbrellas and merchandise lead people into bogus bank verification steps and QR code withdrawals.
items.assessment: The police draw no link to Beijing. Scams and influence campaigns often run on the same rented accounts. A jump in one is a cue to watch for the other before the November 28 vote.

items.headline: Taipei's mayor race heats up, with a Beijing target on the ballot
items.summary: Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an of the Kuomintang, the main opposition party, and his ruling party challenger Puma Shen stepped up campaigning over the weekend. Both also rallied for allies in the Kaohsiung race. The local elections are on November 28.
items.assessment: Police in Chongqing, China, opened a secession case against Shen in 2025, so Beijing has a direct stake in how he does. A strong Shen showing would undercut Beijing's message that its legal threats scare Taiwanese voters.

items.headline: New commanders named at China's regional war commands after purges
items.summary: The South China Morning Post, a Hong Kong paper, reports that new chiefs have been identified at several of the PLA (China's military)'s theatre commands. These are China's regional war commands, including the one that runs Taiwan drills. The posts opened up after the anticorruption purge emptied the ranks.
items.assessment: Commanders promoted fast after a purge rarely take risks on their own. That makes any big Taiwan drill this season more likely to be a political call from Beijing than a local initiative.
items.source: South China Morning Post (via The Star)

items.headline: Beijing vows to protect firms Washington sanctioned over Cuba
items.summary: The US sanctioned Chinese companies it accuses of supplying military items to Cuba. China's foreign ministry said its cooperation with Cuba is fully legitimate. It said it will take all necessary measures to protect Chinese companies.
items.assessment: Cuba is turning into a side front in the US and China sanctions fight just as Washington squeezes Havana. Beijing's wording is the same it has used before announcing its own countermeasures, such as blacklisting US firms.
items.source: PRC Ministry of Foreign Affairs press conference transcript

items.headline: China and Canada reopen a top level economic channel today
items.summary: Vice Premier He Lifeng, China's lead economic negotiator, is jointly leading the second China and Canada Economic and Financial Strategic Dialogue in Canada on November 9. Beijing announced the meeting at its regular press briefing.
items.assessment: Beijing gets a G7 member talking trade with it while US tariffs hit both countries. Watch for Canadian moves on canola tariffs and electric vehicle duties, the two issues that froze ties.
items.source: PRC Ministry of Foreign Affairs press conference transcript

items.headline: Macao jails former lawmaker Au Kam San for 12.5 years
items.summary: Au Kam San, a veteran pro democracy former legislator in Macao, received a sentence of twelve and a half years. Asked by AFP, Beijing's foreign ministry said Macao upholds the rule of law. It warned outside forces not to use court cases to interfere.
items.assessment: Macao rarely draws attention next to Hong Kong, which makes it a quiet test bed. The sentence shows its national security law now produces Hong Kong style penalties for a lone opposition figure.
items.source: PRC Ministry of Foreign Affairs press conference transcript

alsoNoted.headline: Hong Kong police arrest the operator of a prisoner support group over 'seditious' books. Police also switch on AI facial recognition on CCTV this month
alsoNoted.note: Headlines only, not opened

Experts say Taiwan's central bank is struggling to calm the Taiwan dollar after the stock crash
Panamanian lawmaker urges Taiwan to open a trade office in Panama, which cut ties with Taipei in 2017
Hong Kong themed bazaar in Taipei builds ties despite an official freeze between the two governments
A Pakistani astronaut will fly on China's Shenzhou-24 mission
alsoNoted.note: First foreign crew member on a Chinese station mission would be a big prestige gift to Islamabad

items.headline: Myanmar migrants in Thailand boycott the junta's ID document
items.summary: Myanmar's military government admits only about 15,000 migrants have applied for its Certificate of Identity since October 14. It had expected 4,000 to 5,000 a day. The card works as a passport only inside Thailand. Holders must send home 25% of earnings, show payslips and pay a 2% tax on foreign income.
items.assessment: Over two million signatures in one week is a mass refusal to fund the junta, and organizers want the shadow National Unity Government to issue its own ID. Thailand, which has raised the remittance rule with Naypyidaw, now has hundreds of thousands of workers at risk of falling out of legal status.

items.headline: Fishermen say Chinese fish cage operators pushed them off a Pangasinan shoal
items.summary: Small fishers in Sual, Pangasinan, on Luzon's west coast, say operators they describe as Chinese moved hundreds of fish cages onto Calpay Shoal. They say workers chased them off grounds their families have fished for generations. The town agriculture office says it issued no permit for cages there.
items.assessment: This is a sovereignty story inside a Philippine bay, not in the disputed Spratlys, and it is driven by local permits and pollution. Expect China hawks in Manila to use it, which raises pressure for audits of Chinese linked businesses on the coast.

items.headline: Philippine defense chief wants more Marines and bases in the Spratlys
items.summary: Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro called for a bigger Marine Corps and new operating bases in the Kalayaan Island Group, Manila's name for the Spratly islands it holds. He said four brigades are far too few for 7,600 islands. He also said the military must physically hold its own reserve supplies.
items.assessment: The line about holding supplies points to planning for a blockade, where shipments cannot get through. More permanent Marine bases in the Spratlys is the kind of change Beijing will call a breach of the status quo.

items.headline: Belarus and Myanmar's junta deepen ties, from army optics to gemstones
items.summary: DVB examined a 2026 to 2028 cooperation roadmap between Belarus and Myanmar's military government. It covers military optics, assembly of vehicles and tractors, uniforms for security forces, police forensics, bank loans and swaps of gemstones for fertilizer. A company tied to junta leader Min Aung Hlaing's family appears in the deals.
items.assessment: Belarus gives the junta a sanctioned partner outside China and Russia that asks no questions. The gemstone and fertilizer swaps offer a way to trade around Western sanctions.

items.headline: New Zealand's prime minister opens the door to a party he once ruled out
items.summary: Preliminary results give the ruling coalition 67 of 131 seats, just over the 66 needed. Special votes, about 14% of the total, come in with the final count on November 27 and have usually leaned left. Prime Minister Christopher Luxon, who had ruled out the centrist Opportunity Party, now says building a relationship with it is appropriate.
items.assessment: Luxon is buying insurance in case special votes cost him his one seat margin. Opportunity now holds leverage over both blocs for nearly three weeks before any deal can be sealed.

items.headline: Malaysia's attorney general stalls Najib's move to house arrest
items.summary: The Attorney General's Chambers says Najib Razak's house arrest should be suspended pending legal review. It denies defying the King's decree. Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim told the attorney general to seek an audience with the King. Najib's party, UMNO (Malaysia's old ruling party), filed a police report over the delay.
items.assessment: Anwar is letting the legal office, not himself, take the heat from UMNO. The standoff puts the King's pardon power against the courts and keeps Anwar's coalition partners split for weeks.

alsoNoted.headline: Japanese minister blames X's machine translation for a diplomatic near miss
alsoNoted.note: Not opened. Platform translation as a source of diplomatic incidents is a new disinformation vector

alsoNoted.headline: Cambodia revokes 18 casino licences tied to the Prince Group, raids 972 scam sites and deports 23,760 foreigners
Indonesia arrests another official in the case of spying on President Prabowo. Workers rally for him as women march against him
China thanks the Philippines for sending home 115 Chinese suspects from offshore gaming hubs
Myanmar resistance coalition ends a South Korea visit and heads to the Paris Peace Forum
South Korean crypto exchange GOPAX halts withdrawals and trading after hacking threats
alsoNoted.note: Worth checking for North Korean attribution

items.headline: Hasina applies for a Bangladeshi passport and ID card from exile
items.summary: Former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, convicted in absentia and living in India since August 2024, has applied for a national ID card and a passport. Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed says the foreign and law ministries are checking whether she has the right to apply. He said Dhaka has asked for her extradition under the treaty with her host country.
items.assessment: The application is a legal test, not a travel plan. If Dhaka refuses a citizen's basic papers, her lawyers can cite it as political persecution, which is a standard defense against extradition in Indian courts.

items.headline: Bangladesh confirms direct talks with the Arakan Army on Rohingya returns
items.summary: State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam said Dhaka is talking to both Myanmar's junta and the Arakan Army, an ethnic Rakhine armed group. The Arakan Army controls 14 of Rakhine State's 17 townships, including the whole border with Bangladesh. She said diplomacy through normal channels alone will not bring the Rohingya home.
items.assessment: Dhaka is now openly treating a rebel army as the real power next door, which the junta will resent. A former adviser also floated a China backed transit corridor as leverage, which would bring Beijing into the Rakhine deal.

items.headline: Kazakhstan will supply Tajikistan with fuel under 20 new agreements
items.summary: Presidents Kassym-Jomart Tokayev of Kazakhstan and Emomali Rahmon of Tajikistan oversaw 20 documents in Astana. They include a fuel supply framework and business deals worth about US$2.5 billion. Mining also features.
items.assessment: Tajikistan depends on Russian fuel, so a Kazakh supply line cuts some of Moscow's leverage over Dushanbe. It also shows Astana positioning itself as the region's broker.

items.headline: A shrinking Caspian Sea threatens Kazakhstan's trade route to Europe
items.summary: Environmentalist Vadim Ni warns that planning for the Trans-Caspian route, the land and sea path from China to Europe that skips Russia, ignores the sea's falling level. Shallower water limits ships and ports. He also questions the environment ministry's role in the plans.
items.assessment: Western governments are betting on this route to bypass Russia. If ports silt up, the cost rises and Russia's northern rail lines look better again.

items.headline: Kyrgyzstan plans a power hungry industrial park despite chronic shortages
items.summary: Kyrgyzstan's investment agency agreed to a 200 hectare industrial park in Naryn for energy intensive factories and data centers. The country already imports power and rations it in winter. The Times of Central Asia asks where the electricity will come from.
items.assessment: Data centers near the Chinese border would likely serve Chinese clients or crypto mining. Either way they would compete with homes for scarce winter power.

items.headline: Law 186 is now in force: ministers owe merger timetables by about December 9
items.summary: Cuba's government overhaul law took effect today, November 9. It cuts the central government to 20 ministries plus the central bank. The fine print gives each minister 30 days to hand Prime Minister Manuel Marrero a work timetable, and up to one year to move staff, equipment and money. Until another body is named, the new trade and foreign investment ministry also handles consumer protection.
items.assessment: The law names no job cuts and no ministers, so day one changes letterheads more than daily life. The timetables due around December 9 are the first point where outsiders can see which offices and posts really disappear.
items.source: The Rio Times (reading of the Official Gazette text, published November 3)

items.headline: Lula quickly greets Paraguay's new president and offers cooperation
items.summary: Brazilian President Lula publicly congratulated Pedro Alliana, who took over Paraguay after its Senate removed Santiago Peña over the Ueno Bank collapse. Lula said he hopes to work with him in a cooperative way.
items.assessment: Brazil buys most of Paraguay's share of power from the Itaipu dam they own together. Quick recognition from Brasília steadies a neighbor in a banking crisis. It also signals Lula will not treat the impeachment as a coup, unlike the Venezuelan state channel teleSUR, which cheered Peña's fall.

items.headline: Nicaragua now checks the ID of every remittance sender and receiver
items.summary: Nicaragua's Financial Analysis Unit, the state money laundering watchdog, published Resolution UAF-N-027-2026 in the official gazette on November 5. Banks, remittance firms, exchange houses and car dealers must now identify both sender and recipient of every transfer, whatever the amount. They must also check clients against news reports and file secret suspicious activity reports. The stated aim is to unify rules against money laundering and terrorism financing after June reforms on organized crime.
items.assessment: Remittances from exiles are about a quarter of Nicaragua's economy, so the rule turns that money flow into a map of which families are linked to which emigrants. Because a news story can now trigger a financial probe, critics of the government abroad can expose relatives at home simply by being reported on.
items.source: Infobae, citing documents reviewed by Despacho 505

items.headline: Nicaragua frees 2,000 ordinary prisoners on a Sandinista holiday
items.summary: Rosario Murillo, who rules jointly with her husband Daniel Ortega, announced the release of 2,000 inmates convicted of common crimes on November 8. The date marks the 1976 death of Sandinista founder Carlos Fonseca. It is the sixth such release this year, and the government has not said who was chosen or how. The UN counted at least 46 political detainees in July, and the Socialist International put the number of jailed opponents at 72 this week.
items.assessment: Large holiday releases let Managua show mercy while the OAS deadlines on political prisoners run, without freeing a single opponent. The lack of any published criteria also means nobody outside can check whether these releases include anyone held for politics.
items.source: The Rio Times, with Infobae confirming the release on November 9

items.headline: Haitian gang 400 Mawozo asks the UN to mediate as troops close in
items.summary: Wilson Joseph, leader of 400 Mawozo, wrote to the UN Secretary General on November 1 asking for a mediation team. The UN and rights groups accuse the gang of rape, killings and kidnappings, which it denies. Haiti's national disarmament commission replied that any talks must follow the government's roadmap. Police also said Mathias, leader of the Boston gang in Cité Soleil, was killed in a joint operation.
items.assessment: 400 Mawozo is one of two gangs blamed for the October ambush that left four Salvadoran aviation technicians missing. Salvadoran troops began an offensive on its turf in early November. Its sudden offer of talks looks like a bid to bring in the UN and slow down Bukele's troops, who mostly operate outside the UN backed force.

items.headline: Paraguay's new president starts with a $1 billion medicine debt
items.summary: Pedro Alliana, sworn in on November 6 after the Senate removed Santiago Peña, spent his first full day with Health Minister Isaías Fretes on hospital drug shortages. The health ministry owed suppliers about $1 billion as of April, plus $130 million for drug purchases ordered by courts. EFE says the Ueno Bank collapse touched about 2.94 million clients, including state bodies with large deposits.
items.assessment: Leading with medicines gives Alliana a quick visible win that is not about the bank. But state money frozen in Ueno, including pension funds, limits how fast he can actually pay drug suppliers.

items.headline: Taiwan says its ties with Paraguay stay the same under Alliana
items.summary: Taiwan's foreign ministry said relations will remain unchanged after Paraguay's leadership switch. Deputy Foreign Minister Chen Ming-chi said Taipei is in close contact with the government and the ruling Colorado Party. Alliana met Taiwan's ambassador in April and backed the alliance. Paraguay is Taiwan's only diplomatic ally in South America and one of 12 worldwide.
items.assessment: Taipei moved fast because a cash strapped caretaker president is the moment when Beijing's offers look most tempting. Watch whether Taiwan offers money to ease the Ueno Bank fallout, which would be the real test of the alliance.

items.headline: Petro's legal exposure grows: spy agency files and a push to bar him
items.summary: Noticias Caracol, a Colombian TV network, published documents on suspicious contracts, hidden safe houses and staff reshuffles at the national intelligence agency under former president Gustavo Petro. La Silla Vacía, an investigative site, is also discussing whether Congress could formally declare Petro unworthy, a sanction that could bar him from office. A separate scandal over Petro's ties to former Senate contractor Deicy Jiménez led his daughters to say only the courts should decide the truth.
items.assessment: Three months into Abelardo de la Espriella's presidency, the files on Petro are piling up faster than the new government's own agenda moves through Congress. That gives the right a way to keep Petro on the defensive before the next local elections. Petro's response to the intelligence documents was not in what we could read.
items.source: La Silla Vacía (topic page summaries, article pages blocked)

items.headline: Sheinbaum wants a state printer to make Mexico's election materials
items.summary: After the head of Mexico's election authority quit in a contracts scandal, President Claudia Sheinbaum called for a cleanup of the body. She asked the federal auditor to review contracts from every past leadership, not only the last one. She blamed rules kept by the council under former chair Lorenzo Córdova. She also proposed that the government printing house, Talleres Gráficos de México, produce more ballots and voting booths.
items.assessment: Moving production of election materials from private suppliers to a government printer would put part of the 2027 midterm logistics closer to the executive branch. Sheinbaum says this ends a cartel of a few suppliers, while the open question is who would oversee that printer.
items.source: Mexico News Daily (November 6 recap), with details from Animal Político, October 30

items.headline: Pope Leo XIV arrives in Argentina, the home Francis never visited as pope
items.summary: After three days in Uruguay, Pope Leo XIV left Montevideo on Sunday, November 8, for Argentina. In Uruguay he warned about what he called a process of dehumanization. It is the first papal visit to Argentina since John Paul II in 1987.
items.assessment: Francis, an Argentine, never went home as pope, partly to avoid being used in local politics. Leo now faces that same risk with President Javier Milei's government, which will want the images.

alsoNoted.note: Runs to November 2027. Keeps asset freezes and transaction limits available.

alsoNoted.note: Criticism from the global alliance of center left parties, not from Washington. Counts 72 jailed opponents.

items.headline: Officials found little foreign meddling and no vote hacking
items.summary: US officials found minimal covert foreign interference in the November 3 midterms and no sign of hacking to change votes or counts, the New York Times reported. The review covered both influence campaigns and attacks on election systems.
items.assessment: This is the main official answer to claims that machines were rigged, and it comes from an administration whose party lost. Those spreading the claims are more likely to attack the source than the finding.
items.source: Just Security Early Edition (citing the New York Times)

items.headline: DOJ civil rights chief Harmeet Dhillon resigns
items.summary: Harmeet Dhillon, who ran the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, resigned, NPR reported. About 300 career lawyers were pushed out of the division during her time there. The division enforces voting rights, police misconduct and discrimination laws.
items.assessment: Her division runs federal voting rights enforcement, so she leaves in the middle of the post election certification fights. As a private citizen she is also easier for the new Democratic majorities to call as a witness.

items.headline: US charges Jacobo Bucaram in a cocaine trafficking case
items.summary: Federal prosecutors charged Jacobo Abdala Bucaram Pulley, Jaime Estrada Medranda and three others in a cocaine case, AP reported. US Attorney Jamie McDonald announced the charges. Bucaram is a son of former Ecuadorian president Abdalá Bucaram, whose family has faced earlier corruption cases at home.
items.assessment: US prosecutors are now reaching into Ecuador's political families as cocaine flows through its ports. Any extradition request will test President Daniel Noboa's promises of cooperation with Washington.

alsoNoted.headline: DOJ Dobbs leak probe run by US Attorney Jeanine Pirro with prosecutor Carlton Davis
alsoNoted.source: New York Times, via Just Security Early Edition
alsoNoted.note: New detail on who runs the probe reported November 7.

items.headline: Treasury uses cyber sanctions on a Madagascar scam boss
items.summary: The Treasury's sanctions office, OFAC (the US Treasury's sanctions office), blacklisted Chui Kok Wa under its cyber crime program on November 5. Treasury says he ran a scam network in Madagascar that took more than $400,000 from Americans, partly through crypto schemes. The same day OFAC named 45 more people and firms in the Prince Group scam network, including an airline and a hotel in Cambodia.
items.assessment: Naming a small African scam cell shows Treasury now treats overseas fraud against Americans as a sanctions target, not only a police case. It also hints that scam operators are moving to Africa as Southeast Asian compounds face pressure.

alsoNoted.headline: No new OFAC or State Department designations found for November 7 to 9
alsoNoted.note: Weekend. Monday's OFAC page not checked directly.

items.headline: Hardliners push the lame duck to lock in asylum limits
items.summary: Groups backing the administration want the outgoing Republican Congress to write asylum changes and stricter employer checks into law, AP reported. Jeremy Beck of NumbersUSA, a group that favors lower immigration, said Congress will have failed without lasting border legislation. Democrats plan probes of ICE detention warehouses, rushed officer hiring and deaths in custody.
items.assessment: The Senate filibuster makes a lame duck border law unlikely, about a 10% chance. Enforcement money is already locked in for three years, so incoming Democrats can investigate but cannot easily defund.

items.headline: Sudan's army detains ICC fugitive Ahmed Haroun after a podcast interview
items.summary: Sudan's military detained Ahmed Haroun in Omdurman on November 8, according to his lawyers. Haroun led the National Congress Party, the dissolved ruling party of Omar al Bashir. He is wanted by the International Criminal Court for alleged Darfur crimes. His lawyers say the arrest came two days after he appeared on a podcast.
items.assessment: Haroun has openly backed the army since leaving prison in 2023, so his arrest looks like Burhan trimming a visible Islamist ally while foreign sanctions pile up. Watch whether he is quietly released or offered to The Hague, which would tell you how far Burhan will go to please Western and Gulf backers.
items.source: WarHistory.org Sudan event log, citing The New Arab

items.headline: Islamist party chief says Bashir loyalists now own Sudan's war
items.summary: Ali El Haj Mohamed leads the Popular Congress Party, an Islamist party that split from Bashir's movement in 1999. In a Radio Dabanga interview, he said the army has taken on a political role beyond its job. He said the war has become part of the agenda of the dissolved National Congress Party. He called for talks among Sudanese, including the military, and said he is not calling for a coup.
items.assessment: A senior Islamist publicly separating his camp from the army's war gives Burhan cover if he wants to shed his Bashir era allies. It also hints at a split inside Sudan's Islamist world that outside mediators could use.

items.headline: El Obeid's bakeries all shut in a strike over bread prices
items.summary: Every bakery in El Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan state, closed on November 8. Bakers are in a dispute with local officials over bread prices and rising costs. Further east, a farmer in the Gezira farming scheme said large areas of maize died because there was no petrol to run irrigation pumps. A four gallon can of petrol costs about 600,000 Sudanese pounds there.
items.assessment: El Obeid is the army's main hub in Kordofan and sits near the front, so a bread shutdown there is a morale problem, not just a price story. Lost maize in Gezira, Sudan's breadbasket, points to higher food prices next year in army held areas, not only in Darfur.

items.headline: Sudan asks a Sahel and Sahara bloc to label the RSF terrorists
items.summary: At a meeting in Tripoli, Libya, Sudan asked the Community of Sahel Saharan States to designate the Rapid Support Forces as a terrorist group. The RSF is the paramilitary force fighting Sudan's army. The report comes from SUNA, Sudan's state news agency. On the same day the army said it captured Iyal Bakhit in West Kordofan and shot down an RSF drone.
items.assessment: The bloc includes Chad and Libya, both accused of being supply routes to the RSF, so the request is mainly a test of who will refuse in public. A designation is unlikely, about a 10% chance, but forcing members to take sides on the record is the point.
items.source: WarHistory.org Sudan event log, citing SUNA via AllAfrica and Sudan Tribune

items.headline: Uganda starts pulling troops from Somalia as police warn of a gap
items.summary: Uganda has begun withdrawing soldiers from Somalia, where it is a major contributor to the African Union force fighting al Shabaab. A Somali deputy police chief warned of a security vacuum, Hiiraan Online reported. Two days later, Somalia's defence minister met the top US diplomat in Mogadishu about the security handover and the fight against al Shabaab and Islamic State.
items.assessment: The pullout lands in the middle of the fight over the president's expired term, so troops loyal to rival politicians may fill the space before the army does. Washington is now the main outside player Mogadishu can lean on, which raises its leverage over how the term dispute is settled.
items.source: WarHistory.org Somalia event log, citing Hiiraan Online

items.headline: Somali forces fire on Mogadishu protesters over home demolitions, three reported dead
items.summary: Security forces opened fire on residents protesting home demolitions in Deyniile, a district on Mogadishu's edge, on November 8. Three people were reported killed, according to Hiiraan Online. Forced evictions in Mogadishu often hit displaced families living on land that has gained value.
items.assessment: Land grabs during a legitimacy crisis give the opposition a street issue that is not about clan or elections. Deaths at the hands of government forces also weaken the president's claim to be the guardian of order after the court ruling.
items.source: WarHistory.org Somalia event log, citing Hiiraan Online

items.headline: Armed standoff in Beledweyne ends with Hiiraan's governor resigning
items.summary: On November 6 the vice president of Hirshabelle state arrived in Beledweyne with armed supporters. Hirshabelle is a federal member state north of Mogadishu. A leader of the Hawadle clan then urged local security forces to gather in the town, saying the region was under attack. On November 8 the Hiiraan regional governor, Muse Salad Wehliye, resigned over a dispute with Hirshabelle's leaders.
items.assessment: Beledweyne sits on the main road to Ethiopia, and its clan politics now mirror the national split over the president's term. A local power struggle here could pull federal and opposition backers in on opposite sides.
items.source: WarHistory.org Somalia event log, citing Hiiraan Online
