items.headline: Brazil reports a fatal swine flu case with four sick relatives
items.summary: A woman in Santa Catarina, southern Brazil, died of a swine origin flu strain called H1N1v. Four adults in her household also fell ill with flu symptoms but were treated without lab testing. Investigators found no direct pig contact, only a neighbour who keeps pigs. The UK Health Security Agency flagged it as a new event in its November 5 report.
items.assessment: Because the relatives were never tested, nobody can say whether the virus spread person to person, and that question may stay open for good. WHO still rates the risk as low, but the case shows how thin testing leaves a gap exactly where an early warning would matter.
items.source: UK Health Security Agency, outbreaks under monitoring, week 44

items.headline: A second, mild bird flu case follows the first US death in Yakima
items.summary: Yakima County in Washington State reported a second human H5N1 bird flu case on November 1. Unlike the fatal case reported a day earlier, this person was not hospitalised. Both were linked to infected dairy cattle, and the county now has three human cases this year. The US CDC counts 72 confirmed human H5 cases since 2024.
items.assessment: A mild case next to a fatal one suggests many infections among dairy workers go unnoticed, which makes the true count higher than 72. That matters because each human infection is another chance for the virus to adapt.
items.source: UK Health Security Agency, outbreaks under monitoring, week 44

items.headline: Kenya's Ebola cluster quiet since October 19 while Congo keeps climbing
items.summary: Kenya has nine confirmed Ebola cases, including two deaths, and none since October 19, the UK Health Security Agency says. All the later cases were found among people already in quarantine. In Congo, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control counted 10,668 confirmed cases and 5,198 deaths as of November 4. Contact tracing in Congo covers about 84% of contacts.
items.assessment: If Kenya stays clear, it could be declared free of Ebola around December, which would ease pressure on travel rules for East Africa. The one in six contacts nobody is following in Congo is the number that decides whether the outbreak shrinks.
items.source: UK Health Security Agency and European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control

alsoNoted.headline: Nigeria's single imported Ebola case: no new cases, 62 contacts traced
alsoNoted.note: The patient had flown from Uganda via Addis Ababa and was evacuated to Switzerland.

alsoNoted.headline: ECDC Ebola update: Congo adds about 470 cases and 240 deaths in a week

items.headline: Parents sue Google over Gemini on school laptops
items.summary: Parents sued Google, saying its Gemini chatbot on school issued Chromebooks helped their teenager plan a suicide attempt, The Hill reported. The case comes as Google presses schools to accept its AI tools or lose some Search features.
items.assessment: Schools that turn on Gemini to keep Search may end up sharing legal risk for what students do with it. Expect districts to slow adoption until courts decide who is responsible.
items.source: Just Security Early Edition (citing The Hill)

items.headline: A June Supreme Court ruling set Mississippi's Tuesday cutoff
items.summary: In June the Supreme Court ruled 5 to 4 that Mississippi may count mailed ballots postmarked by Election Day that arrive within five business days. That window closes Tuesday, November 10. Mississippi's top election official said about 3,600 outstanding ballots were still expected as of Friday.
items.assessment: A fight over abstract election rules now shapes a Senate seat, and it leaves neither side room to contest late mail ballots. The legal battle will likely move to affidavit ballots, where local officials have more discretion.

items.headline: Judge stops DOJ from forcing Washington to set aside flagged ballots
items.summary: A federal judge issued a temporary restraining order, a short emergency halt, against the Justice Department, Politico reported. DOJ had demanded that Washington state set aside ballots from voters flagged on a federal list of suspected noncitizens. The order keeps those ballots in the count while the case continues.
items.assessment: It is the second court loss in a week for DOJ moves to slow certification, after the Alaska suit was thrown out. The case tests whether a federal database can override a state's own voter rolls.

items.headline: Newsom commutes all 548 California death sentences
items.summary: California Gov. Gavin Newsom commuted every death sentence in the state, 548 in all, to life without parole, the New York Times reported. California has had a pause on executions since 2019, but the sentences themselves had stayed in place.
items.assessment: Acting before he leaves office in January means a successor cannot restart executions without new trials. The move will follow Newsom into any 2028 presidential run, used by supporters and opponents alike.
items.source: Just Security Early Edition (citing the New York Times)

alsoNoted.headline: Four men in the 'Cornell 7' case seek to remove New York AG Letitia James, who names outside counsel Jacqueline Kelly
alsoNoted.source: AP, via Just Security Early Edition

alsoNoted.headline: Late October: DOJ charged two former FBI officials by complaint, skipping a grand jury, and unsealed a third case against Comey
alsoNoted.note: Background only. Several of these cases were later thrown out.

items.headline: Satellite images show Iran digging new tunnels at two missile bases
items.summary: BBC Verify found fresh digging and new tunnel entrances at the Garmdareh and Shahroud missile bases in October imagery. The Critical Threats Project, a research arm of the American Enterprise Institute that tracks the war daily, flagged it on November 6. Iran's logistics minister has said the country will rebuild inside mountains and protected structures.
items.assessment: Iran is moving its missile force deeper underground, so the gains from months of US strikes are wearing off. Any renewed strike campaign would face harder targets than the first one.
items.source: Critical Threats Project and ISW, Iran Update (citing BBC Verify)

items.headline: Kyiv says Russia used the Kherson truce to move about 1,000 troops
items.summary: A Ukrainian brigade spokesperson says Russia used the local ceasefire in Kherson to move about 1,000 troops and equipment. They went onto the occupied left bank of the Dnipro river. The Institute for the Study of War, a Washington research group, reported the claim on November 6. It is a Ukrainian claim and has not been independently confirmed.
items.assessment: If true, the small truce the White House celebrated is working as a supply window for Russia. That will make Kyiv warier of any local pause offered in Abu Dhabi.
items.source: Institute for the Study of War, Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment

items.headline: Russian source says some units near Kupyansk lost half their men
items.summary: A Russian military blogger claims some battalions of Russia's 347th Motorized Rifle Regiment near Kupyansk have lost about half their personnel. The same source says Russia does not control several nearby villages and struggles to resupply. ISW notes the claims are unverified and may not reflect new Ukrainian counterattacks.
items.assessment: Pro war Russian bloggers admitting heavy losses on the eve of Abu Dhabi talks undercuts Moscow's message that time is on its side. It may also be pressure on commanders from inside the Russian camp.
items.source: Institute for the Study of War, Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment

items.headline: Houthis appear to stage toward Aden as Saudi Arabia downs a drone near Mecca
items.summary: Reports on November 5 said the Houthis, the Iran aligned movement that holds northern Yemen, moved equipment to al Turbah, possibly for a push toward Aden. Saudi jets reportedly struck Houthi forces there the same day. On November 6 Saudi air defenses intercepted a Houthi drone near Mecca and two ballistic missiles near Najran, and the Houthis had not denied the Mecca attack.
items.assessment: A Houthi drive on Aden would turn the Yemen front from a Saudi border war into a fight for the south's main port. Silence on the Mecca drone breaks the Houthis' earlier habit of denying strikes near holy sites.
items.source: Critical Threats Project and ISW, Iran Update

items.headline: Syrian military advisers are training Saudi and Yemeni units
items.summary: Under the new Saudi and Syrian defense deal signed November 4 to 6, Syria is sending military advisers to train Saudi and Yemeni government units. The detail comes from the Critical Threats Project's November 6 update. Government aligned Yemeni forces also took positions at Jabal Dahida in Jawf, likely to prepare a push on al Hazm.
items.assessment: Syria's new government is turning its battle hardened officers into an export, which buys it Saudi money and a role in the Gulf. It also means Syrians may end up facing the Houthis in Yemen.
items.source: Critical Threats Project and ISW, Iran Update

alsoNoted.headline: Russia launched 227 drones overnight on November 5 to 6, 86 of them jet powered
alsoNoted.source: Institute for the Study of War
alsoNoted.note: Jet drones are faster and harder for Ukraine's mobile gun teams to catch.

items.headline: Russia will cut parliament staff by up to a fifth to fund the war
items.summary: Sources in Russia's State Duma, the lower house, say it will cut staff by about 15 to 20%. The Federation Council, the upper house, will cut 10 to 15%. The stated goal is to trim nonessential spending as budget deficits grow, after a 15% cut to civil servants in March.
items.assessment: The savings are tiny next to military spending, so the point is the signal. Moscow is asking its own elite to share the cost, a sign the budget is tighter than the Kremlin admits going into Abu Dhabi.
items.source: Institute for the Study of War, Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment

items.headline: Iraq's closed border crossing squeezes Iran's land trade
items.summary: Baghdad closed the al Shayeb crossing with Iran on October 21. Sources said on November 6 that Iran's ambassador, reportedly a member of the Quds Force, the Revolutionary Guards' foreign arm, is pressing for it to reopen. Analysts at the Critical Threats Project say the closure hurts because Iran now leans more on overland trade.
items.assessment: The US naval blockade pushed Iran's trade onto roads, which makes small Iraqi border decisions matter much more. Baghdad now holds a lever Washington wants it to keep using.
items.source: Critical Threats Project and ISW, Iran Update

alsoNoted.headline: Grid capacity prices in the PJM (the grid operator for 13 eastern US states) region rose from $28.92 to $329.17 per megawatt day in two years
alsoNoted.note: PJM is the grid serving 13 eastern states. Its market monitor blamed data centers for 63% of one auction's increase. Gives the bill math behind the data center vote already covered.

items.headline: COP31's top sponsor runs a refinery flat out as its climate goals slip
items.summary: Climate Home News, an independent climate news site, investigated Koç Holding, Turkey's largest conglomerate and a top COP31 sponsor. It reports the group's oil refiner has been running at full capacity while its climate targets slipped. The finding sits in the outlet's COP31 briefing published November 5.
items.assessment: The host's flagship sponsor profits from the high fuel prices the Hormuz crisis created. That will feed doubts about how hard Turkey pushes the fossil fuel language in the final text.

items.headline: Turkey names its electrification pledge signers Tuesday, and India likely stays out
items.summary: November 10 is Energy Day at COP31, when Turkey plans to launch a pledge to get 35% of final energy from electricity by 2035. Today the figure is about 23 to 24%, and current policies reach only about 28%. Australia has signed and Europe likely will, but India is probably a no and China is undecided.
items.assessment: China's choice is the one to watch. If Beijing signs, the pledge becomes a market for Chinese grid and battery gear. If it stays out, the pledge is mostly a European club.

items.headline: COP31 opens with a fight over putting trade on the agenda
items.summary: The UN climate summit opens today in Antalya and runs to November 20. African countries want new agenda items on trade and adaptation money. China wants talks on trade rules that block clean technology exports, and European countries are expected to resist.
items.assessment: The climate talks are turning into a trade forum, where China and Africa press against Europe's carbon border tax. An agenda row on day one could eat days of negotiating time.

items.headline: Even tripled, adaptation money would cover about a third of the need
items.summary: Rich countries refused in Bonn to write a target of tripling adaptation finance by 2035 into the text. A UN report finds tripling would bring $85 to 120 billion a year against about $305 billion in needs. The list of indicators to track adaptation was also cut from 100 to 59 at the last minute.
items.assessment: The fight is over a number that would still leave most of the gap open. Fewer indicators also makes it harder to prove later that money is not arriving.

items.headline: Big emitters set to resist stronger cut language as China and India skip the leaders' days
items.summary: Countries must decide whether the forum on cutting emissions continues, and in what form. Saudi Arabia, Russia, India and China are expected to resist stronger wording. The leaders' segment runs November 11 and 12, and India and China are not sending top leaders.
items.assessment: With the US absent and the two biggest Asian emitters sending junior teams, the summit's weight shifts to Europe, Brazil and small island states. That lowers the odds of binding language.

items.headline: Turkey warns COP31 visitors not to meddle in its internal affairs
items.summary: Attendees were warned not to interfere in Turkey's internal affairs, according to Climate Home News. Government approval for a planned protest was still pending before the summit. Turkey has faced criticism for its crackdown on civil liberties.
items.assessment: Expect friction between activists and Turkish police to become a side story. It also tests whether UN venues still protect protest inside a host country.

items.headline: State economists see $45.8 billion in local losses from Amendment 3
items.summary: Florida's official revenue forecasters project local governments lose $4.95 billion in the first year, rising to $11.86 billion by 2031 to 2032, WGCU reported. That adds up to $45.8 billion over five years. Neighbors are already counting: Sarasota County faces $241 million over two years and Manatee's sheriff more than $50 million.
items.assessment: Lee County's own estimates fall in the same range, so expect hiring freezes and fee increases spread over time, not one big round of cuts. Police and fire make up most local spending, which puts sheriffs at the front of the line for state help.

items.headline: DeSantis wants the special session to block local workarounds
items.summary: Gov. Ron DeSantis said he will call a special session within two months, before his term ends in January, to put Amendment 3 into effect. He wants to stop local governments from making up the loss by taxing residents in other ways, the News Service of Florida reported. School taxes are left out of the bigger homestead exemption.
items.assessment: For Lee County and Cape Coral, the key question is whether fees and special assessments, such as fire or stormwater fees, get capped too. If they do, local governments lose their main backup tool before Governor elect Byron Donalds takes office.

items.headline: Ben Norton: voters rejected the Iran war, Democratic leaders still won't
items.summary: Ben Norton runs Geopolitical Economy Report, a left wing outlet critical of US foreign policy. He argues the Iran war reached voters through gas and grocery prices. He says Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer and House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries remain pro war and pro Israel.
items.assessment: The antiwar left is already turning its fire from Trump to the new Democratic majority. Expect pressure on war funding votes before the new Congress sits in January.
items.source: ScheerPost (republished from Geopolitical Economy Report, Nov 7)
items.support: Exit poll figures he cites: 63% called the Iran war the wrong decision and 51% said US support for Israel is too strong. He cites $55.3 million in pro Israel spending against progressives, including $22.3 million against Abdul El-Sayed, who won in Michigan. He also cites Schumer's 2015 opposition to the Iran nuclear deal and Jeffries declining to call for blocking war money.
items.against: None found. The piece does not name which exit poll produced its figures, and no response from Schumer or Jeffries was found.

items.headline: Prashad: the Sudan, Yemen and Iran wars are feeding each other
items.summary: Vijay Prashad directs Tricontinental, a left wing research institute. He argues the wars around the Red Sea share foreign backers, port rivalries and smuggling routes. He says Sudanese fighters sent to Yemen after 2015 helped build the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), the paramilitary now fighting Sudan's army.
items.assessment: His food angle is the sharp one. About a third of seaborne fertilizer passes Hormuz, so the Iran war raises bread and sorghum prices in Sudan, where 19.5 million already face acute hunger.
items.source: Consortium News (Globetrotter, first published by BreakThrough News on Nov 3)
items.region: Red Sea, Horn of Africa, Gulf
items.support: World Food Programme hunger and price data. A 2019 International Crisis Group report on RSF troops in Yemen. A January 2024 UN expert panel on gold smuggled to Dubai. A May 2025 Amnesty International finding that Chinese bombs used by the RSF were almost certainly resold through the UAE. ACLED conflict data on Emirati troops leaving Socotra. UNCTAD fertilizer figures.
items.against: Abu Dhabi denies supplying the RSF, as the piece itself notes. No other direct rebuttal found.

items.headline: Real News Network says a 2025 Trump memo is jailing protesters for life
items.summary: The Real News Network is a left wing nonprofit video outlet. Reporter Ryan Johnson says left wing protesters face life sentences under domestic terrorism charges. The piece ties this to a September 2025 presidential memorandum telling federal agencies to counter domestic terrorism.
items.assessment: If the reporting holds, the memo is becoming a sentencing tool, not just a policy statement. A Democratic Congress now has a concrete target for oversight hearings.
items.source: ScheerPost (republished from The Real News Network)
items.support: The September 2025 memorandum directing agencies to counter domestic terrorism and organized political violence. Case details were not reviewed because the page could not be opened.
items.against: The White House framed the September 2025 memo as a response to organized political violence. No direct government reply to this piece was found.

items.headline: Hartung and Cortright: Democrats won a mandate for peace
items.summary: William Hartung is an arms trade analyst at the Quincy Institute, a think tank favoring military restraint. He and peace scholar David Cortright read the midterms as a vote against war. They set out four priorities for the new Congress, led by ending foreign wars and domestic repression.
items.assessment: This is the policy wing of the antiwar left writing the new majority's to do list early. Watch whether any Democratic committee chair adopts it.
items.support: The midterm results, read as a rejection of militarism. Details were not reviewed because the page was seen only as a listing.

items.headline: Tucker Carlson declares the end of the Trump era
items.summary: Tucker Carlson is a former Fox News host who now runs his own network. In his midterm episode he called the losses deserved. He blamed the Iran war, living costs and Israel policy, and said Fox News hosts lobbied Trump into the war.
items.assessment: Carlson is making Israel and the Iran war the dividing line of the post Trump right. His talk of a second party gives antiwar Republicans somewhere to go.
items.source: The Tucker Carlson Podcast (transcript via Happy Scribe)
items.support: Exit polls and election results. A post by Vice President JD Vance listing voters' top reasons, led by ending the war. His guest, pollster Rich Baris, said the Epstein files and the war hurt the party.
items.against: In early October the White House called Carlson's Iran criticism misinformed, according to coverage citing NPR and Axios. No reply to this episode was found. His claims about the war's cost and motives are stated without supporting figures.

items.headline: Vaccine skeptic outlets fuse medical examiner emails with a BMJ probe of FDA
items.summary: NaturalNews, a long running alternative health site, merged two stories. One is The Defender's medical examiner emails. The other is a BMJ investigation saying the Food and Drug Administration's (FDA) vaccine safety alarm could not see mRNA harms.
items.assessment: The Defender story now borrows weight from the BMJ, a mainstream medical journal. That makes it harder for health agencies to wave off and likely to surface in new Senate hearings.
items.source: NaturalNews (drawing on The Defender and The BMJ)
items.support: BMJ reporter David Willman on a math flaw that masked signals when Pfizer and Moderna reports were both high. FDA officer Ana Szarfman proposed a fix in March 2021. An October 2023 internal FDA email acknowledged the limit. New York City and Connecticut medical examiner emails obtained under state records law by attorney Jimmy Wagner. FDA emails reportedly obtained by Senate subpoena.
items.against: In the emails, New York City's chief medical examiner wrote she doubted a link in one myocarditis case. The site's own summary says one teen's heart changes resembled stress cardiomyopathy rather than myocarditis. No FDA response was included.
